Skin Incision

Skin Incision
The first, and perhaps the most critical, decision is selection of a safe incision,
particularly in patients who have undergone multiple surgical procedures. Previous
incisions should be clearly marked to ensure they are adequately visualized after the
limb has been fully prepared and draped. Although the use of a long, straight midline
incision is preferred, previous incisions often make this type of incision impossible. To
use or create the safest incision, remember that the vascular supply to the skin overlying
the anterior aspect of the knee is derived from an anastomosis of vessels that run just
superficial to the deep fascia. This vascular supply is asymmetric and primarily originates
from the medial side of the knee. Deep dissection should occur at a level just below the
subcutaneous fascia to maintain skin viability. If possible, large flaps should be avoided
to minimize compromise of the arterial supply to the skin (Figure 1). The following steps
are recommended.1

Figure 1 Illustrations show the vascular anatomy of the thigh. A, Microvascular anatomy
of the skin of the thigh. The vessels just superficial to the deep fascia form an
anastomosis. The skin blood supply arises from this anastomosis, with little
communication in the subcutaneous tissues. The deep perforators (P) supply the
anastomosis above the deep fascia. B, Areas supplied by the deep vessels (solid circles
indicate approximate position of deep perforators). Most of the blood supply comes
from the medial side; therefore, a medial incision will increase the chance of skin-edge
necrosis. (Reproduced from Younger AS, Duncan CP, Masri BA: Surgical exposures in
revision total knee arthroplasty. J Am Acad Orthop Surg 1998;6[1]:55-64.)
Deep Exposure

Deep Exposure
In most revision procedures, a medial parapatellar arthrotomy with complete
synovectomy is performed; however, surgical reports from previous surgeries should be
obtained because some procedures may have been performed via a different approach.
After the arthrotomy, scar tissue should be excised, and adhesions should be released
from the suprapatellar pouch, the medial and lateral femoral gutters, and the dorsal
aspect of the quadriceps tendon proximal to the patella. The proximal tibia should be
exposed to at least the mid-coronal point medially via subperiosteal dissection of the
medial retinaculum and the deep medial collateral ligament. External rotation of the

3/32

flexed tibia reduces tension on the extensor mechanism by displacing the tubercle
laterally, facilitating exposure. Adhesions over the proximal aspect of the tibia, deep and
proximal to the patellar tendon to the anterolateral corner of the tibia, also are released.
At this point, lateral subluxation of the patella is performed, completing the exposure1
(Figure 2).
Figure 2 Illustrations show deep exposure of the knee. A, Appearance of the knee after
exposure with the scar intact. B, Complete exposure is achieved by dissecting out both
femoral gutters and removing the nonpliable scar from the deep surface of the extensor
mechanism. After complete exposure, the distal femur should be visible to the level of
the periosteum, and the undersurface of the quadriceps muscles can be observed. The
collateral ligaments can be dissected as part of a flap off the femur or tibia but should
not be divided transversely at any level. (Reproduced from Younger AS, Duncan CP,
Masri BA: Surgical exposures in revision total knee arthroplasty. J Am Acad Orthop Surg
1998;6[1]:55-64.)

Rectus snip
V-Y quadriceps turndown
Femoral peel
Patellar tendon peel
Tibial tubercle osteotomy
Medial epicondyle osteotomy

Extensile Exposures
In more complex revision procedures, extensile exposure facilitates visualization and
protects the extensor mechanism. The use of these exposures should be minimized
because they are not free of complications.
Rectus Snip
An oblique medial to lateral transection of the rectus tendon at the proximal portion of the
arthrotomy (rectus snip) does not appear to compromise long-term knee function and may
relieve some of the tethering effect of a contracted extensor mechanism2 (Figure 3; Video 1).
The exposure afforded via a rectus snip is not as extensile as that of a V-Y quadriceps
turndown or a tibial tubercle osteotomy.

(A) is used, with additional exposure of the knee obtained by dividing the quadriceps muscle
proximally, with extension of the incision laterally (B). A greater degree of exposure is obtained
with a more distal and transverse cut. (Reproduced from Younger AS, Duncan CP, Masri BA:
Surgical exposures in revision total knee arthroplasty. J Am Acad Orthop Surg 1998;6[1]:55-64.)

V-Y Quadriceps Turndown
A modification of the Coonse-Adams approach described by Insall, this approach allows for
extension of the medial parapatellar approach.
The extension is made in the extensor mechanism 45° to the proximal end of the parapatellar
incision.
Dissection is taken distally through the tendinous insertion of the vastus lateralis and through
the lateral retinaculum.
The blood supply to the patella is possibly maintained through the superior lateral genicular
artery and the vessels within the remaining fat pad supplying the inferior pole of the patella
(Figure 4).
Dissimilar from the quadriceps snip, this approach may result in extensor mechanism
disruption or dysfunction and rarely should be used.

Figure 4 Illustrations of a knee show the incision (A) and exposure obtained (B) with via patellar
turndown. The quadriceps tendon should be repaired with use of a nonabsorbable suture and
should be protected postoperatively. (Reproduced from Younger AS, Duncan CP, Masri BA:
Surgical exposures in revision total knee arthroplasty. J Am Acad Orthop Surg 1998;6[1]:55-64.)
Femoral Peel
Originally described by Windsor and Insall in 1998, the dissections around the lateral and
medial aspects of the femur are continued subperiosteally to include the origin of the medial
and lateral collateral ligaments.3,4
The posterior capsule may or may not be stripped off the back of the femur as necessary,
resulting in complete exposure of the joint and exposure of the distal femur.
The use of a posterior-stabilized constrained implant is required.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 6:01 PM

8/32

The oscillating saw is used in a brush-like fashion to remove the surface layer of fibrous tissue
and cortical bone on the origin and insertion of the ligaments.
Postoperative flexion is restricted to 90° for 8 to 12 weeks postoperatively to avoid dislocation.
Patellar Tendon Peel
Also known as the banana peel approach described by Lahav and Hofmann in 2007, this
technique involves peeling the patellar tendon as a sleeve off the tibia in a medial to lateral
direction, leaving a hinge of the extensor mechanism intact distally and laterally.5
The peel is performed by progressively everting the patella and without the use of sharp
dissection, electrocautery, or a Cobb elevator.
A quadriceps snip also is used in combination with this technique.
At closure, the arthrotomy is closed in a standard fashion over the anterior tibia without the
need to address the peel.
No postoperative precautions are required.
Tibial Tubercle Osteotomy
Originally described by Whiteside in 1990, a long osteotomy of the tibial tubercle in continuity
with the tibial crest and attached anterior compartment muscles maintains vascularity of the
osteotomized bone fragment and a distal soft-tissue tether to prevent proximal migration of
the bone fragment6,7 (Figure 5; Resource 1).
Reliable union rates have been reported via this osteotomy technique (Video 2).
Anterior midline exposure
Tibial tubercle osteotomy is best indicated in patients with adequate tibial bone stock.
Patients with severe osteolysis or osteoporosis of the proximal tibia in whom fixation of the
osteotomy would be compromised may be better treated via a proximal rectus snip.
This approach also may be used to access and remove well-fixed stemmed tibial components.

Figure 5 Illustrations of a knee show the bone cut (A) and the exposure achieved and wire
placement for closure (B) for a tibial tubercle osteotomy. The osteotomy should be at least 8 cm
long and should be as thick as the cortex to allow access to the tibial shaft and to prevent
fracture of the osteotomized fragment. The osteotomy is performed with use of a saw from
medial to lateral and can be completed with the use of osteotomes. The osteotomy is hinged on
the lateral soft tissues, which are left intact to maintain blood supply. The tibial shaft can be
accessed for cement removal, which reduces tension on the extensor mechanism by displacing
the tibial tubercle laterally. The osteotomy is closed by passing two wires through drill holes and
is then stabilized by compression of the cortical bone. The lateral drill holes are placed more
proximal than the medial drill holes to draw the osteotomy distally. (Reproduced from Younger
AS, Duncan CP, Masri BA: Surgical exposures in revision total knee arthroplasty. J Am Acad Orthop
Surg 1998;6[1]:55-64.)

Medical Epicondyle Osteotomy
First described by Engh, the superficial medial collateral ligament and the tissues superior to
the medial epicondyle are raised as a flap, with the medial epicondyle as a bone fragment
within the soft-tissue flap (Figure 6).
Dissection is then performed posteriorly and laterally around the femur and tibia, and the
knee is opened by externally rotating the knee into external rotation and hinging into valgus.
The joint is closed by using a screw to reattach the epicondyle.

Figure 6 Illustration of a knee shows a medial epicondyle osteotomy. The subvastus approach is
used. The medial epicondyle is elevated off the bone with a flap of soft tissue. The flap is then
elevated off the posterior aspect of the femur and tibia, staying on bone. The joint is opened,
hinging on the lateral soft tissues. (Reproduced from Younger AS, Duncan CP, Masri BA: Surgical
exposures in revision total knee arthroplasty. J Am Acad Orthop Surg 1998;6[1]:55-64.)
Management of Bone Defects

Joint line: modular block augments, cement and screws
Metaphysis: cement, impaction grafting, bulk structural allograft, porous metal metaphyseal
cones and sleeves
Diaphysis: cemented versus noncemented stems and short versus long stems
Megaprostheses and allograft prosthesis composite

Management of Bone Defects
Fixation of the revision components must be achieved despite bone defects. The three
zones of fixation are the joint line, metaphysis, and diaphysis. Obtaining solid fixation in
at least two of the three zones has been advocated to allow for early postoperative
mobilization and to improve the longevity of the construct.8,9
Fixation at the joint line typically is achieved with the use of cement; however, in the
revision setting, most fixation typically is in the metaphysis and/or diaphysis.
Occasionally, a metal augment will be used at the joint surface if uneven bone loss is
present; however, it typically is cemented to the bone surface and attached to the
undersurface of the components (Video 3).

Video 3 Lewallen DG: Revision TKA bone deficit management: Screws, cement, graft,
cones and sleeves, from Lombardi AV Jr, mod: Four challenges in revision total knee
arthroplasty: Exposure, safe and effective component removal, bone deficit
management, and fixation. Presented at the Annual Meeting of the American Academy
of Orthopaedic Surgeons, Las Vegas, NV, March 12-16, 2019.
Modular Block Augments
Metal augments are available for reconstruction of tibial and femoral defects.9
These augments are used for uncontained defects measuring 5 to 10 mm.
Augments are recommended if 40% or more of the bone-implant interface is unsupported by
host bone, resulting in instability of the trial implant, or if the periphery of the defect involves
25% or more of the adjacent cortex.
Most revision knee systems offer augments that correspond to the size of the defect and the
size of the implant.
Tibial block augments cover the hemi-plateau or the entire plateau. They may require
additional resection of the host bone for proper sizing. In making the freshen-up cut on the
tibia, the additional resection required for tibial hemi-plateau augments must be made in
correct external rotation. Oversized augments in the tibia will lead to patella baja and must be
avoided.
Femoral augments typically are block-shaped, and the thickness (range, 5 to 10 mm) for the
medial and lateral condyles may vary distally, posteriorly, or both. The need for femoral
augments is evaluated with the placement of a trial femoral implant.
Distal augments are used to re-create the joint line.
Posterior femoral augments are particularly useful in restoring the proper anteroposterior
dimension of the femoral component, establishing proper rotation, and addressing flexion-
extension gap balancing.
Block augments are associated with the advantages of providing immediate support without
the need for consolidation or maturation, shorter surgical time, and immunity to resorption.
Disadvantages of block augments include expense, limitations in size and shape, no bone
stock restoration, and the need to remove additional bone for proper augment placement.
Cement and Screws

Typically reserved for defects that are smaller than 5 mm and comprise less than 50% of the
bone surface area.9
Cement can be used in combination with cancellous screws (3.5, 4.5 or 6.5 mm) for defects
ranging from 5 to 10 mm to enhance load transfer from the prosthesis to the underlying bone
(Figure 7).
The screws should be inserted as pillars to support the implant, with care taken to ensure that
the screw heads are slightly below the level of the implant to avoid affecting implant
alignment.
This is a low-cost alternative to provide good support for small or incomplete defects.

screws. (Reproduced from Sheth NP, Bonadio MB, Demange MK: Bone loss in revision total knee
arthroplasty: Evaluation and management. J Am Acad Orthop Surg 2017;25[5]:348-357.)


Cement and Screws
Metaphyseal fixation may be necessary for filling bone defects and securing implants.
Options include cement or metals, often with a porous surface. Based on the available
literature, no one clear advantageous strategy exists.
Cement
If using cement for metaphyseal fixation, an attempt should be made to interdigitate into the
metaphyseal bone. This can be done with manual pressure.
Occasionally, this bone is sclerotic, and drilling holes or removing the thin layer of sclerotic
bone may allow for better interdigitation.
Impaction Grafting
Impaction grafting of morcellized allograft is performed during revision total knee arthroplasty
to restore bone stock, especially in younger patients in whom future revision procedures are
expected.9
This technique is cost-effective and can be used for various defect shapes.
Disadvantages of impaction grafting include technical difficulty and the risks of intraoperative
fracture, disease transmission, infection, and graft resorption.
Requires careful débridement of the defect with the use of a high-speed burr to further define
the lesion and decorticate the sclerotic base
Contained defects can be managed immediately, whereas uncontained defects require
augmentation with the use of wire mesh.
A trial stem should be positioned in the femoral or tibial medullary canal before firmly
impacting cancellous graft into the defect with the use of a mallet and tamp. The bone is
impacted starting at the tip of the proposed stem, progressing toward the joint. The trial stem
is removed, and the final stem is cemented in place.
Bulk Structural Allograft

Structural allografts can accommodate bone defects of various shapes and sizes.9
The advantages of structural allograft are that it provides good initial support of the prosthesis
and it has the potential to restore bone stock with graft incorporation.
Disadvantages are prolonged surgical time, nonunion, delayed union, disease transmission,
infection, and graft resorption.
The bone defect is cleared of fibrous soft tissue and osteolytic membrane.
The allograft must be placed in warm saline and allowed to thaw before use, and all cartilage
and cortical bone must be removed from the allograft, thereby leaving exposed cancellous
bone.
The graft is treated with the use of a pulse irrigator to remove the remaining marrow elements
from the trabecular bone.
The host bone is prepared to receive the graft, with care taken to avoid removing cortical
bone. Preparation is performed until a solid base for the allograft is attained.
The graft is positioned and provisionally fixed with the use of Kirschner wires.
After the graft is stabilized, an oscillating saw is used to roughly remove the part of the graft
that protrudes above the borders of the defect (Figure 8).
The graft is definitively fixed with the use of cancellous screws, and the final bone cuts are
made.
Additional alterations to the graft can be made to accommodate stems and devices.

Porous Metal Metaphyseal Cones and Sleeves
These are a modern option to manage bone loss without the disadvantages associated with
other reconstruction techniques (eg, disease transmission, nonunion, graft resorption or
fracture).9
In addition to their potential for biologic fixation, these options can be used to fill large defects
and provide immediate additional structural support.
The disadvantages of porous cones and sleeves include the lack of bone stock restoration; the
need to remove additional native bone to accommodate the cone; and, in patients with
periprosthetic infection, challenging implant removal because of biologic fixation.
Cones
The modular cone design allows for management of defects of various sizes and shapes.9
Modern cones are symmetric or asymmetric and can be metaphyseal or diaphyseal.
Various prosthetic devices can be cemented through the inner aspect of a metaphyseal cone.

Cones are secured to the tibial prosthesis with the use of cement. This allows the cone to be
placed independent of the tibial component.
They have porous surface to allow for bone ingrowth.
A burr or special reamer may be used to prepare the host bone to fit the cone.
Sleeves
Sleeves are implant-specific; the sleeves are mated to the revision implant by a Morse taper
and can be implanted without the use of cement.9
Proper implantation of a metaphyseal sleeve requires preparation of the host bone.
A medullary reamer or a trial stem is used to achieve the correct alignment and implant
position.
Broaches are used to prepare the host bone.
The sleeve must be secured to the tibial tray before engaging the Morse taper of the tibial
stem because stems with a diameter greater than 14 mm will not fit through the sleeve
opening.
Removal of a metaphyseal sleeve may be a challenge because of the step-cut design of the
sleeve and its porous coating.
Fixation in the diaphysis can be achieved with the use of stems.
Stem Fixation
Stemmed components are necessary to provide additional implant stability if metaphyseal
fixation is compromised by bone loss or to protect bone grafts from weight-bearing stresses
during postoperative healing.9
Stems may be cemented or noncemented and have variable lengths.
Selection of stem length and fixation depends on many factors, including mechanical stability
of metaphyseal fixation achieved, quality of diaphyseal and metaphyseal bone stock, weight-
bearing capability of bone grafts or augments used, biomechanical demands of the patient,
and amount of implant constraint.
The optimal method of stem fixation in revision total knee arthroplasty continues to be a
subject of debate (Video 4).
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 6:01 PM

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001035

Video 4 Fehring TK: Challenges in revision TKA stem fixation, from Lombardi AV Jr, mod: Four
challenges in revision total knee arthroplasty: Exposure, safe and effective component removal,
bone deficit management, and fixation. Presented at the Annual Meeting of the American

Cemented Stems
Cemented stems provide the important advantage of increasing the surface area of cemented
implant fixation beyond the metaphyseal area and into the diaphyseal bone. They also provide
immediate fixation.9
Although this increases the amount of fixation, it also is associated with the disadvantage of
making fully cemented stems more difficult to remove.
Cemented stems are not canal filling; therefore, they provide the surgeon more latitude in
condylar implant placement, a feature that is helpful in some patients with major anatomic
abnormality. Because they are not canal filling, cemented stems provide less assistance in
guaranteeing limb alignment in most patients with normal anatomy.
Short cemented stems may be combined with metaphyseal cones, eliminating the need for
longer implants.
Cement restrictors should be considered if planning to pressurize cement.
The use of cement also allows for antibiotic delivery.
Noncemented Stems
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 6:01 PM
AAOS | Revision Total Knee Arthroplasty: Surgical Technique
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001035
20/32

Noncemented stems are associated with the advantage of expeditious procedures. In addition,
they are compatible with intramedullary-based revision knee instrumentation systems used by
most manufacturers.9
Most noncemented knee stems are relatively easy to remove.
In addition, if used properly, noncemented stems usually ensure optimal implant alignment
because they are canal filling.
Noncemented stems also are associated with disadvantages.
Most noncemented stems do not have surface treatments designed to gain bone ingrowth or
ongrowth to the stem; therefore, they offload stress from the metaphyseal and condylar
portions of the implant but do not provide true implant fixation.
In addition, noncemented stems do not fit all canal deformities, and in some patients, they
may force implants into positions that create limb malalignment.
Because noncemented stems have to be truly press-fit, they also are associated with risks of
fracture and end-of-stem pain in some patients.
Long Stems
Long stems that engage the intramedullary canal and the diaphysis have been shown to
improve implant alignment but require the use of offset components.
The strength of fixation with short, cemented stems has been shown to be equivalent to that
of long, press-fit stems, particularly with the concomitant use of metaphyseal sleeves and
cones.
Short stems do not require the use offset components.
Megaprostheses and Allograft Prosthesis Composite
Megaprostheses
Megaprostheses are used to replace the entire distal femur or proximal tibia.9
These prostheses are used to treat patients with malignant tumors or severe bone loss, which
typically is encountered after chronic infection or multiple surgical procedures.
They also may be used in patients with a comminuted distal femur periprosthetic fracture to
replace the distal femur.
Allograft Prosthesis Composite
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 6:01 PM
AAOS | Revision Total Knee Arthroplasty: Surgical Technique
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001035

Allograft prosthesis composite is a revision type prosthesis inserted inside a skeletal allograft
in the distal femur or the proximal tibia.
The residual muscles and tendons can be attached to the allograft bone to purportedly reduce
the risk of postoperative instability and provide better function.
The indications for allograft prosthesis composite are similar to those of megaprostheses to
treat patients, particularly young patients, who have undergone large malignant tumor
resection or who have severe bone loss, with the objective of restoring bone.
Allograft prosthesis composite is more technically demanding and associated with the risks of
nonunion, allograft resorption, periprosthetic fractures, and disease transmission.
Implant Constraint
Cruciate-retaining designs
Posterior-stabilized unconstrained designs
Posterior-stabilized constrained designs

Implant Constraint
Revision total knee arthroplasty may be performed with the use of an unconstrained
cruciate-retaining or posterior-stabilized implant, a constrained posterior-stabilized
prosthesis, or a rotating constrained mechanism (Video 5). In general, the use of the
least amount of constraint that provides a stable well-balanced knee is always
preferred.10
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 6:01 PM
AAOS | Revision Total Knee Arthroplasty: Surgical Technique
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001035

Video 5 Thienpont E: Management of instability in revision TKA: Choice of implant & level
of constraint, from Sharkey PF, mod: Revision total knee arthroplasty: Planning and
performance (video technique). Presented at the Annual Meeting of the American
Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, San Diego, CA, March 14-18, 2017.
Unconstrained Cruciate-Retaining Implant
Requires an intact posterior cruciate ligament and collateral ligament support
May be appropriate for revision of failed unicompartmental arthroplasty in a patient with
minimal bone loss and intact ligament supports
Balancing the posterior cruciate ligament is important and must be assessed because it often
is tight or the insertion site may be compromised.
Unconstrained Posterior-Stabilized Implant
An unconstrained posterior-stabilized implant requires intact collateral ligaments, with
balanced mediolateral soft tissues and flexion and extension spaces.
Constrained Posterior-Stabilized Implant
If one or both collateral ligaments are deficient or adequate soft-tissue balance cannot be
achieved, then additional prosthetic constraint is appropriate.
SEND FEEDBACK

A constrained posterior-stabilized prosthesis includes a wide and taller tibial post that fits
tightly into the femoral implant box. This constrains varus-valgus motion and rotation and the
jump distance of the femur.
A rotating constrained prosthesis contains an axle that links the femoral and tibial
components and provides stability to varus and valgus stress but permits rotation.
A constrained posterior-stabilized prosthesis relies on a ultra-high–molecular-weight
polyethylene post to provide constraint, whereas a rotating constrained prosthesis relies on a
metal axle; therefore, rotating constrained prosthesis generally is considered to be more
rigidly constrained, and is indicated in patients with complete loss of collateral ligament
support.
A rotating constrained prosthesis also limits hyperextension; therefore, a rotating constrained
prosthesis may be a better option than a constrained posterior-stabilized prosthesis in
patients in whom the extensor mechanism is deficient because damage to the tibial post may
occur if a constrained posterior-stabilized prosthesis is hyperextended.
Most rotating constrained prostheses require more femoral bone removal than a constrained
posterior-stabilized prosthesis.
Because of the increased torque on the femoral and tibial implants in a constrained posterior-
stabilized prosthesis or a rotating constrained prosthesis, stems should be used to reduce
mechanical loosening.

Tendon Rupture
Acute avulsion of the tibial tubercle intraoperative is best avoided rather than managed.
Exposure of a stiff knee may put the patellar tendon at risk; if the tendon begins to peel off the
tibial tubercle, a towel clip or a metallic pin is placed through the tendon and into the tibial
tubercle.
External rotation of the tibia also will decrease the tension to the extensor mechanism.

If risk of patellar tendon damage is high, a quadriceps snip or other extensile exposure is
indicated.
If avulsion of the patellar tendon occurs, repair with soft-tissue augmentation is preferred.
One technique with reported success is repair with the use of a Krackow stitch secured distally
on the tibia around a screw post and washer. Augmentation with the use of a semitendinosus
tendon graft provides additional biologic healing. After a 6-week period of immobilization in
extension, gradual range-of-motion exercises in a hinged knee brace are initiated, with
controlled flexion increments until full motion and quadriceps strength have been achieved.
An acute rupture of the quadriceps tendon can be repaired end to end in a fashion similar to
that used for nonarthroplasty of the knee. Repair of the tendon should be performed as soon
as possible postinjury.
Primary repair of chronic extensor mechanism disruption without soft-tissue augmentation is
associated with a high risk of failure. The two most common augmentation techniques involve
the use of allograft or a synthetic mesh.
Allograft
Extensor mechanism allograft with the use of Achilles tendon (tendon with calcaneal bone
block in continuity) or a complete extensor mechanism allograft (tibial tubercle, patellar
tendon, patella, and quadriceps tendon in continuity) has been reported most frequently for
the management of extensor mechanism disruption after total knee arthroplasty.
Failure because of intraoperative under-tensioning and graft attenuation may occur.
The graft should be sutured in maximal tension with the knee in full extension, avoiding
intraoperative assessment of the repair by flexing the knee.
Postoperative range of motion is restricted for 6 weeks postoperatively to minimize
complications associated with graft attenuation.
Progressive range of motion is allowed for the next 6 weeks, with ambulation performed in a
brace locked in full extension.
The brace is removed at 12 weeks postoperatively to allow for full activity.
Synthetic Mesh
An uncoated synthetic mesh can be used as an alternative to allograft tissue to reconstruct the
extensor mechanism. Advantages of this technique over allograft include equivalent extensor

Mesh Preparation
A sheet of mesh folded onto itself 8 to 10 times is sewn together with the use of a single
nonabsorbable suture in a running locked fashion.
Distal Fixation
If the tibial component is not going to be revised, then distal fixation of the mesh to the tibia is
achieved via cement and screw fixation through a trough in the tibia tubercle.
If the tibia is being revised, then the mesh is placed anteriorly in the medullary canal, in line
with the tibia crest, immediately before insertion of the tibial component.
Ensure that the mesh is covered by host tissue ventrally and dorsally because the objectives
are for the mesh to scar into the tissue and to avoid abrasion against the implant.
Distal Incorporation
A tunnel is created dorsal to the patella to pass the mesh.
If the tissue superficial to the patella is thin, then elevate the tissue directly off the ventral
surface of the patella, pass the mesh, and close the soft tissue right back to an anatomic
location over the mesh.
Mobilization of the Vastus Lateralis and the Vastus Medialis Obliquus
Mobilize the vastus lateralis and the vastus medialis obliquus distally by releasing all ventral
and dorsal soft-tissue adhesions off the muscle bellies. This requires substantial soft-tissue
dissection proximally.
The goal is to have the vastus medialis obliquus overlap the vastus lateralis by approximately 5
cm.
Unitize Mesh
To fix the mesh proximally, perform a pants-over-vest reconstruction with the vastus lateralis
deep, the mesh in the middle, and the vastus medialis obliquus on top with the use of
nonabsorbable sutures.

Postoperatively, a long leg cast incorporating the foot is applied with the knee flexed to
5°. The cast is changed every 2 weeks, with a total cast immobilization time of 12 weeks.
At 12 weeks postoperatively, the limb is placed in a constrained knee brace full-time for
an additional 3 months. The patient is only permitted to perform active gravity flexion
exercises in the brace, which is adjusted monthly to 45° for the first month, 60° for the
second month, and 90° for the third month, with full–weight bearing permitted during
this time with the brace locked at 0°. During this time and after brace removal, the
patient should use an ambulatory aid, such as a cane, to prevent falls and additional
disruptions to the extensor mechanism.
Patellar Fracture
Patellar fracture after total knee arthroplasty is uncommon, but it may be a considerable
source of morbidity.
Management depends on the integrity of the extensor mechanism, fixation status of the
patellar component, and quality of the residual bone.
Patellar fractures with a stable patellar component and an intact extensor mechanism can be
managed nonsurgically, typically resulting in a good clinical outcome.
Surgical treatment options for the management of patellar fractures with a stable implant and
disruption of the extensor mechanism include extensor mechanism repair, fracture fixation,
partial patellectomy, and complete patellectomy. Studies on surgical fixation for the
management of displaced patellar fractures typically report poor results.
Treatment options for patellar fractures with a loose patellar component depend on the
quality of the residual bone. If the bone quality is good, then implantation of another patellar
component usually is preferred; however, if the bone quality is poor and will not support a
patellar component, then treatment options include removal of the component with partial or
complete patellectomy.

Patellar component loosening may be associated with osteonecrosis of the patella,
malalignment, or fracture.
After removal of the loose patellar component and cement, the remaining bone and the
viability of the patella must be assessed to determine appropriate management.
Reimplantation
If sufficient patellar bone stock is present, then a new, all-polyethylene patellar component can
be cemented in place.
Bone Grafting
If only a shell of cortical bone and insufficient bone stock (<10 mm) remains with adequate
blood supply to the patella, then bone grafting can be performed.12
After the retropatellar surface has been débrided of cement and scar tissue, the sclerotic bone
is burred to expose a bleeding bed.
Scar tissue on the deep surface of the quadriceps tendon and the patellar tendon is
intentionally preserved so this tissue can be used as part of the patellar bone-grafting
procedure.
If adequate local tissue is unavailable, then allograft tissue with fascia lata can be used.
The flap is secured with the use of interrupted non-resorbable sutures, creating a small pouch
with a portal to allow for the insertion and compaction of cancellous bone graft from autograft
or cancellous bone chips.
Ideally, a thickness of more than 20 mm is targeted to restore the quadriceps lever arm and to
account for resorption or remodeling of the bone graft that may occur over time.
Salvage Patellar Button
The indications for a porous tantalum patellar component is a patella with a residual thickness
of less than 10 mm in the thickest segment with at least 50% of the dorsal cortex intact and
vascular bone.
Using a high-speed burr, the host bone is thoroughly débrided, and the remaining bony shell is
then reamed with the use of implant-specific hemispherical reamers.
Trials are used with the goal of restoring normal patellar thickness (26 mm for men and 23 mm
for women).

The tantalum component is secured to the host bone with the use of No. 2 or No. 5
nonabsorbable sutures through drilled holes and is tied down with knots in the dorsal aspect
of the patella.
A standard, three-pegged, all-polyethylene button is cemented to the porous tantalum shell
covering the entire suture ring.
Gull-Wing Osteotomy
For a shell of cortical bone in a nonviable patella, a Gull-Wing osteotomy is a reasonable
treatment option.13
A saw blade is used to make an incomplete midline sagittal osteotomy through the articular
surface (but not through the anterior surface) of the patella.
The medial and lateral borders of the patella are then manually displaced toward the anterior
surface of the patella, greensticking the anterior patellar surface and creating a V-shaped or
gull-wing configuration.
Un-resurfacing
Leaving the residual patellar remnant un-resurfaced also is a viable treatment option.
Patellar Instability
Various technical and design factors may contribute to subluxation and dislocation of the
patella. Important technical factors include the following.
Avoidance of overstuffing the patellofemoral joint
Medial and superior placement of the patellar component
Correct rotational positioning of the femoral and tibial components
Lateralization of the femoral and tibial components without producing overhang
Maintenance of the joint line
Verification of central tracking of the patella via the no thumbs technique
Secure closure of the arthrotomy

Internal rotation of the femoral component must be avoided. The epicondylar axis and
the anteroposterior femoral axis provide fixed anatomic landmarks that facilitate
positioning of the femoral component. Internal rotation of the tibial component creates
external rotation of the tibial tubercle, increasing the quadriceps angle and contributing
to patellar instability. The tibial tubercle is the traditional anatomic landmark for setting
tibial component rotation. Results of surgical management of patellar instability are
good in patients who undergo combined proximal patellar realignment and lateral
retinacular release. Malrotated components can be identified via CT. If malalignment is a
major contributor to patellar instability, femoral and/or tibial component revision must
be considered.

Outcomes
Outcomes of revision total knee arthroplasty are difficult to assess given the
heterogenicity and variability of the techniques that encompass revision total knee
arthroplasty. Some series include single component revision procedures or modular
polyethylene exchanges and others studies do not. Few series have a minimum follow-
up of 10 years. Cases are divided differently with regard to the cause of failure. The
results of septic versus aseptic revision total knee arthroplasty differ, and the results of
revision total knee arthroplasty for the management of instability versus poor motion
differ. No consistency exists in describing the mode of failure, even among registries,
and radiographic reporting is not uniform. In general, patient-oriented and functional
outcomes and satisfaction after revision knee arthroplasty are inferior compared with
those after primary knee arthroplasty. The most common indications for re-revision are
arthrofibrosis, periprosthetic joint infection, and aseptic component loosening.
